corrections: The Python `insert` now stops shifting at the insertion index, so inserting at index 0 works.

corrections: The perimeter walk now goes back up starting one row higher, so the bottom-left corner is not visited twice.

corrections: The small values in the time comparison table are microseconds (they were labeled ns), and a few miscalculated cells were corrected.
The hidden quadratic example now slices the input array, which is what makes it O(n²).

title: Hash Tables | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Learn how hashing maps keys to storage, why collisions matter, and how maps and sets support common interview optimizations.

title: Implement a Hash Table | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Build a hash-table implementation, store and retrieve key/value pairs, and examine how collisions affect correctness and performance.
corrections: `remove()` now deletes the key-value pair from its bucket instead of setting the value to `undefined`, and `insert()` looks for an existing key by scanning the bucket, so a removed key can be added and read again.

title: Catch the Hacker | Coding Interview Question
description: Identify a repeatedly duplicated email by counting frequencies. Compare repeated scans with a map-based pass through the input.

title: Two Sum | Coding Interview Question
description: Find two distinct indices whose values reach a target. Compare pair enumeration with a hash-map solution and test duplicate values.

title: Strings | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Study string traversal, character representation, immutability, and construction costs before practicing text interview problems.

title: Palindromes Permutations Anagrams | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Distinguish palindrome order, permutation arrangements, and anagram frequency counts, then choose the state each text problem needs.
corrections: The Python `is_palindrome` now removes underscores too, matching the JavaScript version.

title: Group Permutations of Palindromes | Coding Interview Question
description: Practice grouping strings by character relationships and reasoning about which arrangements can form a palindrome.

title: Recursion | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Trace recursive execution, define a smaller subproblem, and connect base cases and return values to a clear correctness argument.
corrections: The iterative flatten now puts nested items at the front of its queue, so it keeps the original order: [1, [2, 3], 4] becomes [1, 2, 3, 4].
Tail-call optimization only applies to a call in tail position. Python doesn't implement it, and among JavaScript engines only Safari's does.

title: Find Sum of Digits of a Number | Coding Interview Question
description: Compute a number’s digit sum using arithmetic. Practice recursive decomposition, termination, and tests for single-digit inputs.
corrections: The time and space complexity is O(d), where d is the number of digits, not O(1): Python integers have no maximum size.
The Python solution now uses `number // 10`, so it stays exact for very large numbers.

title: Generate All Permutations | Coding Interview Question
description: Enumerate input arrangements while managing choices and restoring state. Analyze the output size and test small permutation examples.
corrections: The time complexity is about O(n² · n!), not O(n · n!), because strings of up to n characters are rebuilt at each of the n levels of recursion.

title: Logarithms and Time Complexity | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Understand why repeated halving produces logarithmic work and apply that reasoning to search intervals and recursive algorithms.

title: Search and Binary Search | Coding Interview Algorithm
description: Search sorted data by narrowing a candidate interval. Practice boundaries, midpoint updates, and the conditions that guarantee progress.

title: Sorting | Coding Interview Algorithm
description: Compare sorting approaches, runtime assumptions, and the ways sorted order changes an interview problem’s available solutions.
corrections: Merge sort uses O(n) extra space and quick sort O(log n) on average, not O(n log n).
A JavaScript sort comparator must return a number (like `a - b`), not a boolean.

title: Interview Scheduler | Coding Interview Question
description: Work through an interview scheduling problem and practice using ordered information to reduce the search for a valid answer.

title: Shifted Search | Coding Interview Question
description: Find a target in a shifted sorted array by reasoning about ordered intervals and choosing which half can still contain the answer.
corrections: To pick a half, we check whether the target (not the midpoint) falls within the sorted half's range.

title: Sorted Matrix Search | Coding Interview Question
description: Use a matrix’s ordering constraints to reduce the search space. Track boundaries and test targets at edges or outside the data.
corrections: We can eliminate a column because the target is larger than every item above it in that column.

title: Age Sort | Coding Interview Question
description: Explore how a restricted value range can change a sorting problem. Compare counting-based work with general comparison sorting.

title: First Bad Version | Coding Interview Question
description: Find a transition in an ordered sequence using a predicate. Practice binary-search interval definitions and edge-boundary cases.

title: Linked Lists | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Understand linked-list structure, traversal costs, and the pointer relationships behind insertion, deletion, and reversal.

chapters.name: Code Example of a Linked List

corrections: A blockchain links each block only to the block before it, not in both directions.

title: Pointers | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Reason about references, node identity, and reachability so pointer updates do not lose the remainder of a list or tree.

title: Implement a Linked List | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Build linked nodes and list operations, maintain head and tail relationships, and test empty and single-node structures.
corrections: The doubly linked list now starts `length` at 1, since the constructor already creates the first node.

title: Combine Linked Lists | Coding Interview Question
description: Practice combining linked chains while preserving their nodes and maintaining the relationships needed to traverse the result.
corrections: A blockchain is a singly linked list where each block points back to the block before it, not a doubly linked list.
The node class is now `ListNode`, and each block's timestamp is in its `data` field (the video uses `Node` and `timestamp`).

title: Reverse a Linked List | Coding Interview Question
description: Reverse a list by tracking the previous, current, and next nodes. Explain the invariant and handle empty and single-node inputs.
corrections: The node class is now called `ListNode` (the video calls it `Node`).

title: Mirror Delete | Coding Interview Question
description: Work through a linked-list deletion exercise with careful reference updates, boundary checks, and tests that preserve reachable nodes.
corrections: The node class is now called `ListNode` (the video calls it `Node`).

title: Queues | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Learn queue operations, implementation choices, and the role of first-in-first-out order in breadth-first traversal and scheduling.

title: Stack | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Learn stack operations and use last-in-first-out state for nested structures, traversal, and interview problem solving.

chapters.name: The Call Stack and Stack Overflows

corrections: `calculateTax` now returns only the tax (`price * 0.1`), so the total is 1.1 times the price.
A stack overflow means the call stack has outgrown the memory set aside for it, not that the computer is out of memory.

title: Implement a Queue | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Implement enqueue and dequeue behavior while maintaining first-in-first-out order and handling empty-queue transitions.
corrections: A queue can be built on an array (for example a circular buffer). A plain dynamic array is just O(n) at the front, which is why we use a linked list.

title: Implement a Stack | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Implement push, pop, and peek, maintain the top of the stack, and reason about operation costs and empty-state behavior.
corrections: `pop()` returns null only when the stack is empty. Popping the last item returns that item.

title: Max Min Stack | Coding Interview Question
description: Support stack operations while tracking minimum and maximum values. Practice duplicate values and restoring earlier aggregate state.

title: Valid Brackets | Coding Interview Question
description: Validate bracket ordering with a stack of unmatched openings. Test mismatched types, unfinished openings, and closing-first inputs.
corrections: The Python solution now returns False for a closing bracket with nothing to match, like ")" or "())".

title: Trees | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Learn tree terminology and recursive structure, then prepare for traversal, depth, ancestor, and binary-search-tree exercises.
corrections: Binary search tree lookups, inserts and deletes are O(log n) only when the tree is balanced. An unbalanced one can degrade to O(n).

title: Tree Traversal | Coding Interview Algorithm
description: Compare traversal orders by changing when each node is processed. Trace recursive calls and distinguish traversal from search-tree ordering.
corrections: In-order traversal visits nodes in ascending order only for a binary search tree.
The BFS code now returns right away for an empty tree.

title: Binary Search Trees | Coding Interview Data Structure
description: Understand the ordering rules that guide binary-search-tree operations and how tree height affects search performance.
corrections: The smallest and largest values are at the left-most and right-most nodes, which are not necessarily leaves.

title: Implement a Binary Search Tree | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Build a binary search tree, preserve its ordering contract during updates, and test search paths and empty-tree behavior.

title: Binary Tree Max Depth | Coding Interview Question
description: Compute a tree’s depth from its subtrees. State the empty-tree convention and compare balanced and chain-shaped inputs.

title: BST Validate | Coding Interview Question
description: Check the complete binary-search-tree ordering rule, including ancestor constraints that a parent-only comparison can miss.

title: Closest Common Ancestor | Coding Interview Question
description: Find the shared ancestor of two nodes by reasoning about subtree results and the relationship between node identity and ancestry.

title: Depth First Search | Coding Interview Algorithm
description: Traverse a graph by following branches, track visited nodes to handle cycles, and reason about recursive or explicit stack state.
corrections: The iterative DFS now marks a node as visited when it is popped from the stack, not when it is pushed, so it always follows a path to its end before backtracking.

title: Breadth First Search | Coding Interview Algorithm
description: Traverse by distance with a queue, avoid duplicate discoveries, and reconstruct shortest paths when edges have equal cost.
corrections: The Python BFS now tracks visited nodes in a set, so checking whether a node was visited is O(1).

title: Implement a Graph | Coding Interviews and Computer Science
description: Represent vertices and edges, maintain neighbor relationships, and prepare a graph structure for traversal and reachability queries.

title: Robot Maze | Coding Interview Question
description: Determine whether a robot can reach an exit under the allowed movement rules. Practice grid bounds, blocked cells, and path choices.
corrections: The brute-force recursion uses O(r + c) space for its call stack, not O(2^(r + c)). The memoized solution's O(r × c) space comes from its memo.

title: Subproblems and Overlapping Subproblems | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Identify repeated smaller decisions and define state precisely before using caching or a dynamic-programming table.

title: Memoization | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Turn repeated recursive work into reusable results. Choose complete cache keys and distinguish missing results from valid zero values.

title: Bottom Up vs Top Down Algorithms | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Compare memoized recursion with tabulation, choose a valid evaluation order, and reason about stack and table storage.
corrections: The bottom-up `fibonacci` now returns n when n < 2, so `fibonacci(0)` is 0, the same as the top-down version.
Tail-call optimization does not make most top-down solutions constant space.

title: Dynamic Programming | Coding Interview and Computer Science
description: Develop a recurrence, identify repeated states, and connect memoization and tabulation to interview problem-solving strategies.

corrections: The solution now returns 0 for any negative board length before building its memo, so lengths below -1 no longer crash.

title: Steal Packages | Coding Interview Question

corrections: The four-house example said [5, 10, 20, 50] gives 55, but the best is 60, so the example now uses [10, 5, 20, 50].
